issues.legal_issue: A suit for specific performance is timely when the parties have extended the performance period and the suit is filed within three years after the plaintiff receives notice that performance has been refused.
material_facts: The sale agreement stated that the balance payment was due within fourteen months, but the company’s title to the property was not clear and proceedings to resolve title continued.
The purchaser sent repeated requests for a sale deed, and the company gave assurances, including a letter shortly before the refusal that it would honour the agreement.
The courts below found that the parties had extended the time for performance and that the company refused performance on 21 August 1985.
The purchaser filed the specific-performance suit soon after the refusal.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because the performance period had been extended and the suit was filed soon after the company refused performance.
issues.legal_principle: Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, requires a suit to be filed within three years from the date fixed for performance; if no date is fixed, the period runs from when the plaintiff has notice of refusal. Where a date was originally fixed but the parties extend the time, including by conduct or forbearance, limitation runs from notice of refusal. Section 63 of the Contract Act, 1872, permits a promisee to extend the time for performance, and the extension need not be written. The Court applied S. Brahmanand v. K.R. Muthugopal, R.K. Parvatharaj Gupta v. K.C. Jayadeva Reddy and Gunwantbhai Mulchand Shah v. Anton Elis Farel; it distinguished Ramzan v. Hussaini, Tarlok Singh v. Vijay Kumar Sabharwal, T.L. Muddukrishana v. Lalitha Ramchandra Rao and Venkappa Gurappa Hosur v. Kasawwa C/o Rangappa Kulgod on their facts.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and performance_time_extended and refusal_notified and suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.performance_time_extended: The parties extended the time for performance, as shown by their agreement or conduct.
predicates.refusal_notified: The plaintiff received notice that the defendant refused to perform the agreement.
predicates.suit_filed_within_three_years_of_refusal: The plaintiff filed the suit within three years after receiving notice of refusal.

issues.definition: When a specific-performance plaintiff files within three years after notice of refusal, an extension of the performance period means the suit is not barred by limitation.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot introduce on appeal a new limitation theory that depends on factual matters not pleaded or tried below and would have required an issue and evidence.
material_facts: The appellant argued before the Supreme Court that limitation should run from the date the company’s title was perfected.
That theory had not been raised before the courts below, and the parties had adduced evidence on a different basis.
The Court observed that the proposed theory could have required an issue to be framed and evidence to be adduced.
issues.conclusion: The appellant could not raise the title-perfection limitation theory for the first time before the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: Limitation is a mixed question of law and fact, and its application depends on the agreement and the parties’ conduct and understanding. A new factual theory that was not raised below and would have required an issue and evidence cannot be introduced for the first time in the Supreme Court. The Court applied Article 54 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and considered the approach described in Gunwantbhai Mulchand Shah v. Anton Elis Farel.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party challenged a civil judgment in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.limitation_theory_not_raised_below: The party did not advance the particular limitation theory before the lower courts.
predicates.theory_requires_factual_issue_or_evidenc: Deciding the new theory would require factual findings, an issue for trial, or evidence not addressed below.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a limitation theory not raised below is not entertained when deciding it would require factual findings or evidence that were not addressed in the lower courts.

issues.legal_issue: A contract for sale is not void for uncertainty when its terms are not vague, and an uncertainty challenge not raised below cannot be introduced for the first time on appeal.
material_facts: The appellant argued in the Supreme Court that the agreement’s terms were uncertain and therefore void.
The uncertainty argument had not been raised in the lower courts.
The Court found on reading the agreement that its terms were not uncertain or vague.
issues.conclusion: The uncertainty challenge could not be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, and the agreement was not uncertain or vague in any event.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, concerns agreements whose meaning is not certain or capable of being made certain. The Court declined to entertain the challenge because it had not been raised below and, independently, held that the agreement’s terms were not uncertain or vague.

predicates.civil_appeal: A party challenged a civil judgment in an appellate proceeding.
predicates.uncertainty_challenge_not_raised_below: The party did not argue in the lower courts that the agreement was uncertain.
predicates.agreement_terms_clear: The agreement’s terms are not vague or uncertain.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, an agreement with clear terms is not void for uncertainty even when the uncertainty challenge was not raised below.

issues.legal_issue: A company may be bound by a sale agreement executed in its name by its directors with authority, despite the absence of a separate resolution or the company seal.
material_facts: The company’s directors entered into the sale agreement in the company’s name, and the courts found that all the directors had executed it.
The company’s later correspondence showed that its directors knew of the agreement, and the company did not deny its terms or dispute that it was binding.
The company was a party to the agreement, and the acts of its directors were not found to be ultra vires or contrary to public policy.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was enforceable against the company notwithstanding the asserted failure to comply with Sections 46 and 48 of the Companies Act, 1956, including the absence of a separate authorising resolution or seal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 46 of the Companies Act, 1956, provides for contracts made on a company’s behalf by a person acting with express or implied authority; Section 48 addresses a company’s authorisation of a person to execute deeds on its behalf. Section 46 concerns the mode of signing contracts, and a company may be bound where the evidence shows that the contract was made on its behalf with authority. An oral agreement for sale is permissible, and the absence of a seal does not by itself prevent liability where the transaction and the authority of those acting for the company support it. The Court relied on Chairman, Life Insurance Corporation v. Rajiv Kumar Bhasker on agency, and referred to Probodh Chandra v. Roadoils (India) Ltd. and OTV Birwel Co. Ltd. v. Technical and General Guarantee Co. Ltd. on liability despite absence of a seal.

rule.if: specific_performance_suit and company_sale_agreement and directors_executed_for_company and company_knowledge_or_acceptance and directors_had_authority and not ultra_vires_or_public_policy

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A plaintiff brought a suit seeking specific performance of an agreement.
predicates.company_sale_agreement: The agreement for sale was made in the name of a company.
predicates.directors_executed_for_company: The company’s directors signed the agreement on the company’s behalf.
predicates.company_knowledge_or_acceptance: The company knew of the agreement or acted in a way accepting it, and did not dispute that it was binding.
predicates.directors_had_authority: The directors acted with express or implied authority to enter into the agreement for the company.
predicates.ultra_vires_or_public_policy: The directors’ act was outside the company’s powers or contrary to public policy.

issues.definition: A company is bound by a sale agreement made in its name when its directors executed it with authority, the company knew of or accepted it, and the act was neither outside the company’s powers nor contrary to public policy.
